subject: anatomy
title: Popliteus Muscle, Unhappy Triad, Knee Bursae, and Drawer Testing

steps.tx: The **popliteus** muscle is a flat triangular muscle lying in the deep floor of the popliteal fossa. Uniquely, it arises intracapsularly from a pit on the lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle, passes beneath the fibular collateral ligament, and emerges through the joint capsule to insert into the triangular area of the posterior tibia.
steps.say: The popliteus is a triangular muscle on the deep floor of the popliteal fossa. Originating intracapsularly from the lateral femoral condyle, its tendon passes beneath the lateral collateral ligament to insert onto the posterior tibia.

steps.tx: Referred to as the key to unlock the knee joint, the popliteus initiates flexion from the fully extended locked posture. When standing with the foot planted, popliteus contracts to **laterally rotate the femur** on the tibia, releasing the taut cruciate and collateral ligaments so that the hamstring muscles can proceed with knee flexion.
steps.say: Regarded as the key that unlocks the knee, the popliteus initiates flexion from complete extension. On a planted foot, it contracts to laterally rotate the femur on the tibia, relaxing the locked ligaments.

left.title: Closed Kinetic Chain (Planted Foot)
points: Tibia is fixed against the floor
Popliteus laterally rotates the femur on tibia
Unlocks tightened cruciate and collateral ties

right.title: Open Kinetic Chain (Free Foot)
points: Femur is stabilized by body weight
Popliteus medially rotates the free tibia
Initial movement before swinging limb flexes
Also protects lateral meniscus by retracting it

steps.tx: A severe lateral blow to a flexed, weight-bearing knee with the foot planted produces the catastrophic **unhappy triad** of O'Donoghue. Excessive valgus strain coupled with external femoral rotation sequentially tears three vital structures: the tibial collateral ligament (MCL), the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL), and the medial meniscus.
steps.say: A violent lateral blow to a flexed knee produces the unhappy triad of O'Donoghue. Severe valgus stress combined with external rotation tears the medial collateral ligament, anterior cruciate ligament, and medial meniscus.

steps.tx: Anterior and posterior stability of the knee are assessed by the **drawer test**. With the knee flexed to ninety degrees and the patient's foot stabilized, the examiner pulls the proximal tibia anteriorly: anterior displacement greater than six millimetres indicates an ACL rupture, while posterior subluxation on pushing backward confirms PCL deficiency.
steps.say: Anterior and posterior knee stability is evaluated using the drawer test. With the knee flexed to ninety degrees, excessive anterior translation indicates an ACL tear, while posterior sag reveals a PCL rupture.

left.title: Anterior Drawer Test
points: Pathologic forward glide confirms ACL tear

right.title: Posterior Drawer Test
points: Pathologic backward glide confirms PCL tear

steps.tx: Chronic friction or trauma over the anterior aspect of the knee provokes distinctive bursitis syndromes. Inflammation of the subcutaneous bursa situated between the skin and the lower half of the patella is known as **prepatellar bursitis** (housemaid's knee), resulting from prolonged kneeling with the torso leaning forward.
steps.say: Repetitive anterior knee trauma provokes distinctive bursitis syndromes. Swelling of the bursa between skin and the patella produces prepatellar bursitis, classically termed housemaid's knee.

steps.tx: A fluid distension of the bursa interposed between the semimembranosus tendon and the medial head of gastrocnemius is termed a **Baker cyst** (popliteal cyst). Communicating directly with the knee synovial cavity, increased synovial fluid production from rheumatoid arthritis or chronic meniscal tears forces fluid into the cyst through a valve-like slit.
steps.say: A Baker cyst develops when the bursa between the semimembranosus and medial gastrocnemius becomes distended. Because it connects to the joint space, arthritis or meniscal tears force excess fluid into the mass.

nodes.label: Excess Synovial Fluid Elevates Intra-articular Pressure
One-way Slit Valve Channels Fluid into Semimembranosus Bursa
Tense Popliteal Mass and Pseudothrombophlebitis Risk

steps.tx: Perfusion around the knee joint is sustained by the **genicular anastomosis**, an intricate collateral network surrounding the patella and femoral condyles. This anastomosis is formed by nine arteries: five genicular branches of the popliteal artery, descending genicular from the femoral, descending branch of lateral circumflex femoral, and anterior and posterior recurrent branches of the anterior tibial artery.
steps.say: Blood flow around the knee is safeguarded by the genicular anastomosis. Formed by nine arteries, it links popliteal genicular branches with femoral and tibial recurrent vessels.

steps.tx: Ruputure of a Baker cyst allows synovial fluid to extravasate downwards into the calf tissues, provoking acute calf erythema, induration, and tenderness that mimics deep vein thrombosis. Clinically designated **pseudothrombophlebitis**, urgent compression ultrasonography differentiates ruptured popliteal cyst from occlusive calf venous thrombosis, sparing the patient unnecessary anticoagulant therapy.
steps.say: Rupture of a Baker cyst causes synovial fluid to track down into the calf, mimicking deep vein thrombosis. Termed pseudothrombophlebitis, duplex ultrasound distinguishes the fluid collection from venous thrombosis.
